new_statements.quote: In this chapter, I argue that Haruai has a language internal phonological correlate of the head-dependent relation, namely that, in the absence of other factors (contrastive stress, greater stress associated with focus, that is, essential new information), dependents receive greater stress than their heads. The basic wordstress rule in Haruai is for stress to fall on the first syllabic segment of the word; the only consistent exceptions are negative verb forms, which are stressed on the negative morpheme, for example n dw-lm-a ‘I did not go’, literally ‘I go-NEG-PAST(-1.SG)-DEC'.
new_statements.citation: Comrie, Bernard. 1993. The phonology of heads in Haruai. In Greville G. Corbett, Norman M. Fraser & Scott McGlashan (eds), Heads in Grammatical Theory, 36-43. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511659454.003
new_statements.locator: p. 36 (opening paragraph, section 'Introduction'; displayed as the chapter 'Summary' on the Cambridge Core page)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: the full quoted passage is present verbatim in (Cambridge Core chapter page for Comrie 1993, 'The phonology of heads in Haruai', Heads in Grammatical Theory pp. 36-43, DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511659454.003; the page shows 'Summary' = the chapter's opening 'Introduction' paragraph). Grep hits for 'basic wordstress rule', 'first syllabic segment' and 'stressed on the negative morpheme' (2 each, page body + metadata); the tag-stripped text reads: "The basic wordstress rule in Haruai is for stress to fall on the first syllabic segment of the word; the only consistent exceptions are negative verb forms, which are stressed on the negative morpheme, for example n dw-lm-a 'I did not go', li…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllabic segment of the word (the first syllable as phonetically realised, since Haruai semivowels have syllabic and non-syllabic allophones and consonant clusters are broken by a non-phonemic epenthetic vowel). The one consistent exception is the negative verb form, where stress goes to the negative suffix (Comrie 1988: 154 likewise: 'the suffix -öl, always stressed').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the accessible paragraph.
new_statements.exceptions: Negative verb forms are stressed on the negative morpheme; contrastive stress and focus stress can override the phrasal pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule; separately, at phrase level, dependents receive greater stress than their heads (the chapter's main claim). Statement taken from the open first paragraph of an 8-page chapter; the full chapter (paywalled) presumably gives more detail.
new_statements.identity_note: Comrie's 'Haruai' (earlier 'Harway'/'Wiyaw') is the language haru1245 as a whole, based on his fieldwork among the Haruai of the Schrader Ranges (Wovan/Waibuk area, south-west Madang Province); dialect (North/Central/South Waibuk: nort2926/cent2122/sout2946) not specified in the sources opened. Some database records list the 1998 switch-reference chapter under the editor's name 'Janse, Mark' — it is by Comrie.
